prize_parts.citation: for discoveries in GLP-1 physiology and the development of long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonists that transformed the treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings placed GLP-1 first, which tells us about consensus on importance but not on credit, and I treat those as separate questions. On importance there is little to argue: proglucagon processing, the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36) amide, and receptor biology led through a continuous, independently confirmed chain to liraglutide and semaglutide, with large randomized outcome trials showing glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal benefit. It is a complete arc from basic endocrinology to a new therapeutic class and is still expanding, so recognition is timely. For the allocation I keep Holst (physiology of GLP-1 secretion and action) and Drucker (GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology and the translational rationale) as the scientific anchors, and I keep Knudsen because the clinical achievement exists only because acylation-based half-life extension made the peptide usable. A citation that names both physiology and the development of agonists represents that chain honestly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the trio is contestable. Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) form is a real contribution with a disputed priority history, and Habener is not on the supplied list. Naming Knudsen, an industrial scientist, over Mojsov could be read as favouring drug engineering over discovery, and leaving out Mojsov could be read as ratifying a contested attribution. Three names cannot carry all the credit, and any choice leaves a defensible claimant out. Long-term durability and safety of obesity therapy are also still accruing, though the efficacy data are strong enough that this does not alter my view.

responses.point: Linnarsson favours the basic-discovery trio of Drucker, Holst and Mojsov for GLP-1, and in B041 prefers a two-person June and Sadelain configuration, placing Rosenberg outside it.
responses.response: I take the GLP-1 argument seriously and it is the point on which I am least sure of my own ballot. Where we differ is on what the prize is for. The Mojsov case rests on identifying and synthesising the active peptide, a step that is both important and disputed in priority, whereas the long-acting analogue is the step without which there is no drug to credit. If the committee wants a purely discovery-level prize I would accept the Mojsov trio, but then the citation must not imply the therapy, and I doubt a discovery-only citation matches how this field's impact is judged. On CAR-T I agree with you that Rosenberg is the weakest of the three for CAR specifically, since his work is adoptive transfer and TIL, but dropping him does not solve the Eshhar originator question, so I would not treat the two-person version as cleaner on attribution.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks GLP-1 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov and describes Knudsen's pharmaceutical development as the engineering step rather than the discovery, with credit allocation between Mojsov and others contested.
responses.response: I disagree that the analogue is merely engineering. Native GLP-1 has a half-life of minutes, and converting it into a once-daily and then once-weekly drug required real insight into albumin binding and acylation, which is a scientific contribution in its own right and was decisive for the outcome trials that justify the prize. I agree with you that the allocation is unresolved, and that the Mojsov question cannot be settled from the supplied text. Where I would move is on one point. If the committee decides the prize should recognise physiology only, then your trio is the more defensible one, and I would not object to it on principle.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, supports Drucker, Holst and Knudsen for GLP-1 and notes that Mojsov's priority is a contested credit that he cannot verify from the supplied material.
responses.response: We are aligned on the configuration, but I want to avoid two of us agreeing by default. The risk in our trio is that it can look like an exclusion of Mojsov rather than a principled line, so the committee should state the principle explicitly: Holst and Drucker for the physiology and biology, Knudsen for the translation into usable agonists. I would also guard against your view of B017 as an equally strong first choice. Imatinib is a very strong paradigm but already widely honoured, and I do not think it is as clear a case of an unrecognised achievement as GLP-1.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranks GLP-1 first with the Drucker, Holst and Mojsov triplet, and places Knudsen as a major contributor beyond the three-person limit, while ranking TNF and IL-6 cytokine blockade highly as clean two-person cases.
responses.response: I agree that the credit is crowded, and your point about Habener is fair, since his absence from the supplied list means we are working within an imperfect set of names whichever trio we choose. I would resist treating Knudsen as beyond the limit: the limit forces choices, and the question is whether the prize reflects the discovery or the therapy, not whether he is a contributor. On B043 and B035, I accept that they are mature and cleanly attributed, but they sit well below GLP-1 in impact and breadth, and I would not move them above CAR-T or the unfolded protein response on that basis alone.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants a discovery-level prize (Drucker, Holst, Mojsov) or one that also recognises pharmaceutical development (Knudsen), and how to treat the contested Mojsov priority.
Whether Habener's absence from the supplied credit should change how much weight we place on the proposed names.
For the alternative B041, whether the unresolved originator question (Eshhar and others, outside the supplied credit) makes any three-person configuration unsafe.
Whether long-term safety and durability of incretin therapy in obesity will change how the achievement is described in the citation.
statement.conflict_note: I have documented co-authorship with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisén in single-cell work, and my postdoctoral RNA-processing work was done with Christopher Burge's group at MIT. None of these touches the shortlisted candidates I am proposing, and none is a formal mentor or supervisory tie, so no specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I note for transparency that my scientific field is close to B008 (antisense correction of SMN2 splicing), which I did not choose for the preferred configuration or the alternatives.
